newsitem.title: USA: Okla. City defendants seek to be tried separately.
newsitem.headline: Okla. City defendants seek to be tried separately.

text.p: The alleged co-conspirators in the Oklahoma City bombing case face a key hearing Wednesday when their attorneys try to convince a federal judge to order separate trials for each man.

Defence teams have argued in court filings that the trials must be severed to insure fairness because the strategies of each defendant will surely be "antagonistic" to the other -- that is, they may point the finger of guilt at each other.
The lawyers will also argue that each defendant incurs the risk of "spillover prejudice" if the two are put on trial together.
U.S. District Judge Richard Matsch has set aside three days for the hearing to give lawyers for defendants Timothy McVeigh and Terry Nichols a chance to argue for separate trials.
"We are guardedly optimistic," McVeigh's attorney Stephen Jones said about the possibility of severance.
But prosecutors say two trials would be more expensive and time consuming than one, and the only way to paint a complete picture of the crime for the jury is to try both men together.
The trial was moved to Denver because of the difficulty of insuring a fair hearing in Oklahoma. No date for the trial has been set, but it is expected to get underway in early 1997.

Prosecutors also claim two trials would present a hardship for the relatives of the 168 people who died and the hundreds of others injured at the April 19, 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal buidling.
Defence lawyers said they fear they may actually assist the prosecution by pointing the finger at the other defendent in arguing his own client's innocence.

Matsch has ruled that statements Nichols made to investigators when he gave himself up to police in Kansas can be used only against himself, and not against McVeigh. The statements have been edited out of the court papers the public sees, though prosecutors have said the information is not that damning against McVeigh.
But attorneys for McVeigh argue that jury members would be engaging in "mental gynmastics" by trying to remember that certain evidence can only be used against one defendant.

Matsch recently said he would allow prosecutors to seek the death penalty. As a result, defence attorneys will argue that the risk of their client's death makes it even more imperative for the defendants that separate trials be granted.
But the defence faces a daunting challenge in trying to convince the judge to hold two trials.
"It's very hard to get a trial severed in federal court and very, very hard in the 10th circuit," said local attorney and newspaper columnist Andrew Cohen, referring to Colorado's federal district.
Case law in the district says even if a defendant would face prejudice the judge can remedy the problem by giving proper instructions to the jury, Cohen said.
Nichols' defence team has suggested as an alternative that two juries be impaneled. Prosecutors have said this is not necessary, but an option they could live with.
